cues.en: Welcome, everybody. Thanks for coming to this session. So I'm Evan Juplicki. I'm the designer of the Elm programming language, and I got started on it about seven years ago with a paper called Elm Concurrent FRP for Functional GUIs, and I was like, I really think I can make this functional programming stuff easier, and I didn't nail it immediately with that title, but I had this idea of
cues.zh: 大家好，欢迎来听这场演讲。我是 Evan Juplicki，Elm 编程语言的设计者。大约七年前，我发表了一篇题为《Elm Concurrent FRP for Functional GUIs》的论文，由此开启了这个项目。当时我觉得，我真的能让函数式编程变得更简单；虽然光看那个标题我并没能完全做到，但我有了这样一个想法：

cues.en: This experience with typed functional programming that was really joyful and what I wanted to get out with Elm was like I wanted to take that part that I felt was so fun and make it accessible to other people and share that joy that I had felt. And so part of that is technical. You know you have to write a compiler and all this kind of stuff. But another part is like practical stuff like getting set up should be easy and that was part of what was important to me.
cues.zh: 那种类型化函数式编程的体验真的太棒了，而我想通过 Elm 做到的，就是把我觉得特别好玩的部分提取出来，让其他人也能轻松接触到，分享我感受到的那种乐趣。这其中一部分是技术层面的，比如你得写一个编译器之类的；但另一部分是实用层面的，比如环境搭建必须得简单，这也是我认为很重要的部分。

cues.en: having spent a whole day just trying to learn something trying to see if something was interesting and being really frustrated. Another piece of that was if program is going to be fun I want the community friendly. I didn't want it to be a cool club for the cool kids. You know we're functional programmers and you're not because you're dumb. Like I didn't I didn't relate to that. I just had a nice time programming and I wanted to share that nice time in the same way that I like sushi and I might say hey.
cues.zh: 谁都不想花上一整天去学新东西、看看它到底有没有意思，结果搞得灰心丧气。另一方面，如果编程要变得有趣，我希望社区也是友好的。我不想让它变成少数“酷小子”的精英俱乐部，说什么“我们是函数式程序员，你不是因为你太笨”，我完全不认同这种态度。我只是很享受编程的快乐，想把这种快乐分享出去，就像我喜欢吃寿司，就会跟人说：

cues.en: You should try it out. It's pretty nice. And so I might say, no thanks. Oh, OK. That's the kind of interactions I wanted to have, because it was just about having this experience. So as I've talked to more open source developers, people who design languages, people who work on databases, people who work on machine learning or discussion platforms or environmental sensors, however much we disagree on design or what
cues.zh: “你应该尝尝，味道真的很棒。”对方要是说“不用了，谢谢”，我就会说“噢，好吧”。我想要的就是这种交流氛围，因为重点纯粹在于享受这种体验。随着我和越来越多的开源开发者交流——做语言设计的、做数据库的、做机器学习的、做讨论社区或者环境传感器的——不管我们在设计或目标上有多大的分歧，

cues.en: where our goals are. We all have stories in common about like having a friendly community is really really difficult. And that's one of the places in open source where you know as good as you can be at the technical stuff like you don't have a lot of you ultimately you can't control what's going to happen if someone's going to yell it's like I wish that didn't happen. So I've been doing this for about seven years now and I've started to notice some patterns of behavior that I think.
cues.zh: 我们都有一个共同的体会：维持一个友好的社区实在太难太难了。这也是开源领域的一大痛点，就算你技术再厉害，归根结底你也无法完全掌控局势；如果有人跳出来大吵大闹，你只能叹口气希望这种事别发生。做开源大概七年了，我开始注意到一些行为模式，我觉得

cues.en: probably a lot of people who have worked in open source with larger prize will relate to. So one is this, why don't you just? And in Elm, it's like why don't you just get the JS API directly? Or release an incremental version instead of a bigger release? Or hey, can we derive JSON decoders? And the short answer in all these cases is that it's more complex than it sounds. Like if there's something that you can think of in five minutes or an hour or a day,
cues.zh: 很多做过大型开源项目的人大概都会深有同感。其中一种就是：“你为什么不直接……？”在 Elm 里，经常有人问“你为什么不直接调用 JS API？”或者“为什么不发个小修小补的增量版本，非要憋大版本？”又或者“能不能自动派生 JSON decoder？”对于所有这些问题，简短的回答就是：事情远比听起来要复杂。如果你花五分钟、一小时或者一天就能想出一个方案，

cues.en: probably someone has thought about that and considered it. And there might be implications that you don't see from your perspective, but someone else in the community might have a problem with that that's not obvious to you. So when you're doing design, you know, why don't you just, it's like, well, there's all these different parties that we have to sort of make things work for. And I can do my best on my intuition, but ultimately, even after I spend like a week trying to design something that way, I need to go out and show it to people and see what objections they bring.
cues.zh: 大概率早就有人想到过并且仔细权衡过了。站在你的角度可能看不到某些潜在影响，但对社区里的其他人来说可能就是个严重的问题，只是你没有意识到。所以在做设计时，面对那些“你为什么不直接……”，现实是我们必须去协调照顾各方需求。我可以凭直觉做到最好，但归根结底，哪怕我花上一周按那种思路做好了设计，我也得拿出来展示给大家，看看他们会提出哪些反对意见。

cues.en: And then maybe do it with another design. So this why don't you just is like it's quite frustrating. And one thing that happens is there's a lot of people who are new to the project. So maybe there's 10,000 people who might be curious like oh why don't you just try out this kind of thing. And the number of people who know the full context is pretty small. So maybe there's like 10 20 people. So if it takes five minutes to say why don't you just blah blah blah. And it takes two pages of writing.
cues.zh: 然后再用另一种设计来做。所以这个“你为什么不干脆……”真的很让人沮丧。一个情况是，有很多人刚接触这个项目。可能有 1 万人会好奇：哎，你为什么不干脆试试这种方案呢。而真正了解完整背景的人却很少，可能也就 10 个、20 个。所以，如果说一句“你为什么不干脆 blah blah blah”要花五分钟，而写清楚却要两页纸。

cues.en: And you have to write it very carefully, because if you're an influential community member, people will refer back to what you said four or five years ago and say like, man, there's such a jerk. Here's the evidence. They said this in 2013. And it's like, yeah, yeah, yeah, I said that in 2013. Yeah. Yeah. So one thing that's common is like, well, if it's so much work, why don't you just?
cues.zh: 而且你还得写得非常小心，因为如果你是有影响力的社区成员，人们会翻出你四五年前说过的话，然后说：天哪，这人真讨厌。证据在此，他们在 2013 年就这么说过。然后你只能：对对对，我 2013 年确实说过。对对。所以常见的一种反应就是：好吧，如果这活儿这么多，你为什么不干脆……？

cues.en: delegate the work, right? So this is a comment I got in real life. And the italics are from the person talking to me. They said, there's another way to deal with this, like delegation. And then they go on to describe how delegation works and what benefits it might have. And I was like, oh, very interesting. Yes, I hadn't thought about that. And they describe a person who can do all this work. And they say, this somebody, again, that is their italics.
cues.zh: 把工作委派出去，对吧？这是我现实中收到的一条评论。斜体是跟我说话的那个人自己加的。他们说：还有另一种处理方式，比如委派。然后他们继续描述委派怎么运作、可能有什么好处。我当时想：哦，很有意思。是啊，我还没想到这一点。然后他们描述了一个能做完所有这些工作的人。他们说，这个“某个人”——再次说明，斜体是他们加的。

cues.en: can also be a proxy who's gathering feedback. So you don't have to be in these discussions. So I was initially very upset about this. So the unfiltered in my own mind version was like, oh, hello, is this the somebody store? Yes, we'd like someone to take unsolicited advice on the internet. Oh, yeah, it's really mean. Yeah, it's going to be rough. And yeah, no one's going to say thank you.
cues.zh: 也可以是一个代理，帮你收集反馈。这样你就不必参与这些讨论。所以我一开始对此非常不爽。我内心里没过滤过的版本是：哦，你好，这里是“某个人商店”吗？对，我们想找个人来接收网上不请自来的建议。哦对，这话真刻薄。是啊，这差事会很艰难。而且没人会说谢谢。

cues.en: Yeah, no, it's unpaid. Yeah, it's unpaid. It takes, yeah, it takes... You don't have any... I was told there would be somebody who would do this. And, you know, so this was me in my own life, like, walking around my room, just like... And that's, you know, that's not a healthy place to be. That's not how I want to look to a community. That's not what I want the community I'm a part of to be either. And when I...
cues.zh: 对，不，这是无偿的。对，无偿。它要花，对，要花……你没有任何……有人跟我说过会有某个人来做这件事。你知道，这就是我在现实中的状态：在房间里走来走去，就像……你知道，那不是一种健康的状态。那不是我想要在社区里呈现的样子。那也不是我希望自己所属的社区变成的样子。而当我……

cues.en: took some time and thought about it more, I realized there's actually like a pretty reasonable assumption going on here, which is like free rice means you can take as much as you want. The rice is free. Take a lot of rice. And so does that imply that free labor means you can use as much as you want? Well, the labor is free. But in fact, this isn't how labor works. If you don't pay for labor, you get less. And so I think that's sort of the root thing. It's like, oh, well, it should be unlimited. Anyone can help. Now,
cues.zh: 花了一些时间，再多想了想之后，我意识到这里其实有一个挺合理的假设：免费米饭意味着你想拿多少就拿多少。米饭是免费的，多拿点。那么这是否意味着免费劳动力就是你想用多少就用多少？嗯，劳动力是免费的。但实际上，劳动力不是这么运作的。如果你不为劳动力付费，你得到的会更少。所以我觉得这差不多就是根源：哦，那它应该是无限的，任何人都能帮忙。现在，

cues.en: Let's assume it is unlimited, that everybody in the world actually can't help. In practice, you actually have to work together. These are highly technical projects. Are you able to work well together? Is your goals with the project aligned? How much time does it take to coordinate with that person to get stuff done? So even if you can work with anybody you want, there's still these limitations on who is going to be really effective in doing the right stuff. So I wrote about that a little bit in this post. I think
cues.zh: 假设它是无限的，而世界上每个人实际上并不能都帮上忙。现实中，你还是得一起协作。这些都是技术性很强的项目。你们能很好地合作吗？你的目标和项目一致吗？和那个人协调把事情做完要花多少时间？所以即使你可以想和谁合作就和谁合作，仍然会有这些限制：谁才能真正有效地做正确的事。所以我在这个帖子里稍微写了写。我觉得

cues.en: Or no, sorry, Richard wrote about that in this post here, of like, what actually does it take to get involved? And it's like, it's not just the somebody store. So, you know, some people may be thinking like, you know, Evan, you're doing a lot of telling us what's the situation, but like, who are you to say that? And so this is another pattern that I see a lot, is like, on whose authority?
cues.zh: 或者不，抱歉，是 Richard 在这篇文章里写了这件事，讲的是真正参与进来到底需要什么。大概就是，这不只是“某个人商店”的事。所以，你知道，有些人可能会想：Evan，你说了很多情况给我们听，但你是谁，凭什么这么说？所以这是我经常看到的另一种模式：你凭什么？

cues.en: And this is actually the title of a post that was sent to the Closure community. And the post started out, F Closure. There I said it, and God feels good. I say it with much admiration and respect to all the community members. And then they go on to say some criticisms and talk about the relationship with women. And it's quite a roller coaster of a post. But what's...
cues.zh: 这其实是一个发到 Closure 社区的帖子标题。帖子开头是“F Closure。我说出来了，天啊，感觉真好。”我这么说其实满怀对社区成员的钦佩和尊重。然后他们继续提出一些批评，并谈到与女性的关系。这个帖子真是跌宕起伏。但什么……

cues.en: interesting, besides sort of like it as a journal entry, is that it gets a lot of engagement, right? So 320 comments on the Reddit thread. I'm sure people talked about it in other contexts as well, where there would have been more comments. And, you know, as someone who's been working on an open source project for a bunch of years now, enough people have told me that Elm is going to die next month.
cues.zh: 有意思的是，除了它有点像日记，它还获得大量互动，对吧？Reddit 帖子上有 320 条评论。我肯定人们也在其他场合讨论过，那里评论会更多。而且，你知道，作为一个做开源项目多年的人，已经有足够多的人告诉我 Elm 下个月就要死了。

cues.en: that I'm like, I don't think they're right this time. I have that fear doesn't speak to me anymore because I have the experience. But there are other people in the community who don't have that same experience. And this can be a scary thing of, man, people aren't liking this thing. Are we doing something wrong? They feel like maybe it could be better. They might get defensive. So in one of these 320 comments, the creator of Closure says,
cues.zh: 以至于我会想，这次我不觉得他们说得对。那种恐惧已经不再困扰我了，因为我有经验。但社区里还有其他人没有同样的经验。这会很吓人：天啊，大家不喜欢这个东西。我们是不是做错了什么？他们觉得也许它可以更好。他们可能会变得防御。所以在这 320 条评论中的一条里，Closure 的创建者说：

cues.en: I found out about this while sitting down to spend my weekend contributing to the closure ecosystem. Time spent in lieu of spending time with my wife, having already spent my work week on other closure related stuff. And I relate to this a lot. I've definitely written like, hey, I get there's different viewpoints, but we can't yell our viewpoints at each other. And that was my Saturday. And as you work,
cues.zh: 我是在坐下来准备利用周末为 Closure 生态做贡献时发现这件事的。这些时间本来可以用来陪我妻子，而我已经把工作周花在其他 Closure 相关的事情上了。我对此很有共鸣。我肯定写过类似的话：嘿，我明白有不同观点，但我们不能互相冲对方吼观点。那就是我的周六。而随着你工作，

cues.en: over the course of the years, like, there can only be so many Saturdays that are like that before it starts to hurt you in larger ways. So, Rich Hickey goes on to say, you know, every time I have to process a diatribe like this in its aftermath, the effects on myself, my family, and my coworkers, I have to struggle back from why should I bother? And every time it gets harder to justify to myself and my family that it's worth the time, energy, and emotional burden.
cues.zh: 经过这些年，这样的周六只能有那么多，之后它就会在更大的方面伤害你。所以 Rich Hickey 接着说，你知道，每次我不得不在事后消化这样一篇长篇抨击，它对我自己、我的家人和同事的影响，我都得努力从“我为什么还要费心？”中挣扎回来。而且每次我都越来越难向自己和家人证明，这值得投入时间、精力和情感负担。

cues.en: Now, I've talked to some people about this post, and they thought different things stood out. To me, this last part is what stands out because I think a lot of people in open source feel this way and would never say it out loud. I was really surprised to see it that way, and it kind of gave me some confidence to talk about that kind of stuff as well. So, you know, we have our posts like this in the Elm community with a bunch of...
cues.zh: 现在，我和一些人谈过这个帖子，他们觉得突出的地方不一样。对我来说，最后这部分最突出，因为我觉得很多开源中的人有这种感觉，却永远不会大声说出来。看到它被这样说出来，我真的很惊讶，这也给了我一些信心去谈这类事情。所以，你知道，我们在 Elm 社区也有这样的帖子，还有一堆……

cues.en: comments as well. And I see it not just as like, oh, man, this is hard for me to process, but the people I work with have a hard time processing it. And then if you just add up all the time, let's say maybe 10 minutes is spent on each of these comments, which I think is low, like a conservative estimate. We're talking about like 50 hours for this one. That's just like dealing with someone's anger and...
cues.zh: 还有那些评论。在我看来，这不仅是我自己觉得难以消化，连我的同事们也同样难以承受。如果把所有时间加起来，就算每条评论花 10 分钟处理——我觉得这都算保守估计了。光是应付这一个人，我们大概就要花上 50 个小时。全都在处理别人的怒火，还有……

cues.en: Could that have been helping someone new or spending time with some family members or like learning some hobby that could get you out of work and get you like a more healthy attitude? So one thing I hear a lot when I talk about this stuff is like if it makes you so mad, why don't you just not read it? Why don't you just not read it? So another pattern that's really common is that all discussion is constructive.
cues.zh: 这些时间本可以用来帮助新手、陪伴家人，或者培养一点爱好，让你从工作中抽离出来，保持更健康的心态不是吗？所以在聊起这些事时，我常听到一种说法：“既然这让你这么生气，那你干嘛不索性别看？别看不就得了？”此外，还有一个非常普遍的思维模式：所有讨论都是具有建设性的。

cues.en: I'm just saying how I feel. I feel like F you, and I respect you a lot. And I think you're an idiot, but I really learned a lot from you. And that's a difficult personal relationship to have. I don't know if people have people like that in their life, but that's a difficult thing to deal with a lot. So one discussion that was along these lines is, should Elm have user-definable infix operators? This came up recently with a recent release.
cues.zh: 就比如：“我只是说说我的感受。我想说去你的，但我又非常尊重你；我觉得你是个白痴，但我确实从你身上学到了很多。”这种人际关系处理起来非常心累。我不知道大家生活中有没有遇到过这种人，但要经常去应对真的很折磨人。最近就有一次类似的讨论：Elm 是否应该支持用户自定义中缀运算符？这是在最近的一个新版本中提出来的。

cues.en: And if we just focus on this question, like textually, someone might say, yeah, there are cases where it makes code shorter and more convenient. And someone else might say, no, because it can make code harder to read, especially in a large team. And textually, this is an interesting argument. Yeah, it can make code shorter. That's a good point. And it might hurt people in a large team. And then onlookers will sort of say, oh, which one seems to make more sense to me?
cues.zh: 如果我们单看这个问题本身的字面意思，有人可能会说：确实，在某些情况下它能让代码更简洁、更方便；另一个人可能会说：不行，因为这会让代码更难读，尤其是在大团队中。字面上看，这个争论很有意思。没错，它能让代码更短，这是个好论点；而且它确实可能会给大团队带来困扰。围观的人就会琢磨：“嗯，哪一方听起来更合理呢？”

cues.en: But when you take a step back and stop thinking of it just as like a textual argument about who's right and who's wrong, and say, okay, all these people have different priorities, some of them may value flexibility a lot, and some people might value simplicity a lot, and all these people exist on this with different priorities. So the person who's like, yeah, we should have this, really might value flexibility. And the person who says no is saying, well, if...
cues.zh: 但当你退一步看，不再把它单纯当成关于谁对谁错的字面争论，而是认识到：好吧，大家看重的优先级各不相同。有些人可能极其看重灵活性，而有些人可能极其看重简洁性，每个人都有着不同的关注点。因此，赞成“对，我们应该支持这个”的人，可能真的非常看重灵活性。而反对的人则会说，如果……

cues.en: Like all these benefits you're telling me about flexibility or like how code can be shorter and more convenient It's like that's not persuasive to me like that's not a good rational argument because it's just not important And it's likewise, you know, how does it work on a large team? It's like well that doesn't this doesn't matter. It's not about that And all the people exist on this spectrum is or with different parties as well So they're evaluating it not as which is the true objective argument, but given my priorities
cues.zh: “你跟我说的灵活性带来的所有好处，或者代码能多么简短便捷，根本无法说服我，这对我来说根本不算合理的论据，因为这压根不重要。”反之亦然，“在大团队里表现如何？这根本无所谓，关键不在这儿。”每个人都在这个光谱的不同位置，各有各的立场。因此，他们评判的标准并不是哪方才是客观真理，而是基于自己的优先级……

cues.en: which is the one that makes the most sense to me. So I've come to see constructive discussion is about mutual understanding rather than mutual agreement. And a lot of discussions online are like, we're going to get to a point where you agree with me, rather than saying, huh, this person's seeing it different. Why is that? Maybe they're seeing something I don't. So when I take a step back and think about these different patterns, I just think, why?
cues.zh: 哪一种对我而言最合理。所以我逐渐意识到，建设性的讨论是为了达成“相互理解”，而不是“达成共识”。网上的很多讨论却像是在争“非要让你赞同我不可”，而不是去思考：“咦，这个人的看法不一样，为什么呢？也许他看到了我没注意到的东西。”所以当我退一步审视这些不同的思维模式时，我就会想：为什么会这样？

cues.en: Why is this happening? You know, I don't have problems like this in normal life. You know, if I'm at an Elm conference or a meetup or like nothing ever is so emotionally difficult as these interactions. So I found this documentary called All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace by Adam Curtis. It's excellent, as is all of his work. And that sort of taught me or I found through that a book called
cues.zh: 为什么会这样？你知道，我在日常生活里没这种问题。你知道，如果我在 Elm 大会、聚会之类的地方，没什么互动会像这些一样在情绪上这么难。后来我找到 Adam Curtis 的纪录片《All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace》。它非常棒，他的作品都这样。这算是教会了我，或者通过它我找到了一本书，叫

cues.en: from counterculture to cyberculture. So this revealed to me sort of an intellectual history going back to the 1950s that really helps explain what's going on in open source right now. So it traces things from a book called The Human Use of Human Beings. So this came out of MIT in like 1952 by a person who had created
cues.zh: 《From Counterculture to Cyberculture》。这向我揭示了一段可追溯到 1950 年代的思想史，真的有助于解释开源现在发生的事。它从一本叫《The Human Use of Human Beings》的书开始追溯。这本书大概 1952 年出自 MIT，作者曾创造出

cues.en: artillery that could automatically track planes and shoot them down. And then the whole earth catalog, which was popular in the back to the land movement, so a lot of people on communes might have bought this, but it was a much larger thing than that. And then finally, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and it sort of ties these together in a very interesting way. So we'll look at some of the things going on here. So in the human use of human beings, Norbert Wehner,
cues.zh: 能自动追踪并击落飞机的火炮。然后是《Whole Earth Catalog》，它在“回归土地”运动中很流行，所以很多住在公社的人可能买过，但它的影响远不止如此。最后是 Electronic Frontier Foundation，它把这些以很有趣的方式串了起来。我们会看看这里发生的一些事。那么在《The Human Use of Human Beings》里，Norbert Wiener

cues.en: introduces the idea of cybernetics. He defines it as the study of messages as a means of controlling machinery and society. It's a little weird. OK. OK, fine. And as you start to read it, it's like this way of like, let's not look at the person, but let's look at the messages going around, and that's how we'll think about how the world works. And so you see things like words such as life, purpose, and soul are grossly inadequate.
cues.zh: 提出了控制论的概念。他把它定义为研究信息，以此作为控制机器与社会的手段。这有点怪。好吧，行吧。你开始读的时候，它像是这样一种方式：别盯人，盯周围流动的信息，我们就这样思考世界如何运作。于是你会看到类似这样的话：生命、目的、灵魂这些词都严重不足

cues.en: to precise scientific thinking. Which is, it's like fair enough, but also like those things like life and purpose are like pretty important to people as well to consider. But, you know, a person's just a special sort of machine, right? Like we can consider it as a thing that takes inputs and does stuff. Emotions are just a useless epiphenomenon. That's real, he said that.
cues.zh: 对精确的科学思维来说。这话吧，也算有道理，但生命、目的这些东西对人们来说也挺重要，值得考虑。不过你也知道，人只是一种特殊的机器，对吧？我们可以把它看成一个接收输入、做事情的东西。情绪只是无用的副现象。这是真的，他真这么说过。

cues.en: Another thing is like we have modified our environment so radically that we must now modify ourselves in order to exist in this new environment. So it's sort of how can we take a person and simplify it down to a machine or a system that we can understand well. And then once we're starting to think of people that way well we can improve machines we can add things to them and the machines get more capabilities. Maybe that's how we move forward as people and life and purposes like that.
cues.zh: 另一件事是，我们把环境改变得太彻底了，现在必须改造自己才能在这个新环境里存在。所以问题有点像：我们怎么把人简化成一台机器、一个我们能很好理解的系统？一旦开始那样看人，好吧，我们就能改进机器、给它们加东西，机器能力越来越强。也许人类、生命和目的之类的东西就是这样向前发展的。

cues.en: We can't go back to that. It's too different now. So the sort of connecting thread and whole earth catalog, besides Stuart Brand, the author of this, knowing a bunch of the people in the cybernetics group, is this idea of access to tools, right? So like, we are now, our relationship with our tools is gonna be how we move forward. So this catalog starts with, we are as gods and we might as well get good at it.
cues.zh: 我们回不去了。现在太不一样了。所以《Whole Earth Catalog》的一条连接线索，除了作者 Stuart Brand 认识控制论圈子里的一堆人之外，就是“获取工具”这个理念，对吧？也就是说，现在我们与工具的关系将决定我们如何前进。这本目录开头就是：我们如同神，那我们不妨把神当得好一点。

cues.en: So far, remotely done power and glory as government, big business, formal education, church has succeeded to the point where the gross defects obscure actual gains. In response, personal power is developing. So he's focused on a bunch of different topics. And so education, finding inspiration, shaping his environment, sharing the adventure.
cues.zh: 到目前为止，由政府、大企业、正规教育、教会所遥控的权势与荣耀，其成就已经到了重大缺陷掩盖了实际成果的地步。作为应对，个人力量正在崛起。所以他专注于一系列不同的话题：教育、寻找灵感、塑造个人环境，以及分享探索历程。

cues.en: Now, keep in mind this is written in 1969. So this is before the Internet. And if you read these points as like what an ideal view of the Internet should be, it works really well. Like, you can find out all sorts of interesting stuff. You can be inspired by what's going on out there. You can find a place where you really fit in, even if you don't fit in, in your local community that has different values than you. And you can share that with whoever you want to. Like, there's this place for self-expression.
cues.zh: 请记住，这是写于 1969 年的内容，也就是互联网诞生之前。如果把这些观点看作对互联网理想形态的畅想，其实非常贴切。比如，你能发现各种有趣的事物；你能被外界发生的一切所启发；就算你在价值观不同的本地社区格格不入，也能找到真正属于自己的天地；你还能随心所欲地与他人分享——这里成了自我表达的乐土。

cues.en: And so he says, tools that aid this process are sought and promoted by the whole earth catalog. So some people have argued that this is sort of like what preceded the internet. It sort of foresaw what was going to happen there. And this publication and the creators too at Brand have been really influential. So one of the positive quotes is, when I was young, there was an amazing publication called The Whole Earth Catalog, which was one of the Bibles in my generation. So that was Steve Jobs.
cues.zh: 因此他说，助力这一过程的工具正是 Whole Earth Catalog 所探寻并推广的。所以有人认为它就像是互联网的前身，预见了未来的发展。这本刊物及其创作者 Stewart Brand 影响深远。比如有一段著名的评价：“我年轻时，有一本不可思议的刊物叫 Whole Earth Catalog，它是我们那代人的圣经之一。”——说这话的正是 Steve Jobs。

cues.en: There was a project that Stewart Brand created called the 10,000 Year Clock, which Deaf Bezos helped fund with $42 million. So what is this book that was popular on Back to the Land Communes became very influential because of this, how tools and like a rejection of hierarchy were somehow in this new place where we're gonna choose our own future through our connection with tools.
cues.zh: Stewart Brand 还发起过一个叫 10,000 Year Clock 的项目，Jeff Bezos 曾出资 4200 万美元支持。这本曾在“重返土地”公社运动中风靡的书之所以极具影响力，正是因为它展现了工具和对层级制度的摒弃，如何在这个新空间里让我们通过与工具的联结，自主选择未来的道路。

cues.en: And finally, the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Interestingly, the founders of this met on the whole earth electronic link, one of the earliest message boards. And so one of the founders wrote the Declaration of Independence of Cyberspace. Governments of the industrial world, you weary giants of flesh and steel, you have no sovereignty where we gather. I declare the global space
cues.zh: 最后是 Electronic Frontier Foundation。有趣的是，它的创始人们相识于最早的 BBS 之一 Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link。其中一位创始人写下了《赛博空间独立宣言》：“工业世界的政府，你们这些血肉和钢铁筑成的疲惫巨人，在我们聚集之处，你们毫无主权。我宣布，我们正在建立的全球……

cues.en: social space we are building to be naturally independent of the tyrannies you seek to impose on us. So again, you see this distrust of hierarchy. Big business has failed. Government has failed. We are going to find a new way through this thing. So one of the early cases that the Electronic Frontier Foundation that inspired the creation of this foundation was there was a programmer called Lloyd Blankenship. And Bell South found it.
cues.zh: ……社会空间，天然独立于你们企图强加给我们的暴政。”所以你再次看到了这种对层级制度的不信任。大企业失败了，政府也失败了，我们要另辟蹊径。启发成立 Electronic Frontier Foundation 的早期案例之一，就涉及一位名叫 Lloyd Blankenship 的程序员，当时 BellSouth 盯上了他。

cues.en: some of their 911 alert system documentation had been posted on a bulletin board, and so they got the secret service involved and took some computers that might have sensitive information. So Lloyd was arrested, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation was created around that time to help protect people in this situation. So after Lloyd was arrested, he wrote something called the Hackers Manifesto, which I think gives a rawr version of what's going on in this world.
cues.zh: 他们的一些 911 警报系统文档被贴到了公告板上，于是他们让 Secret Service 介入，并带走了一些可能含有敏感信息的电脑。所以 Lloyd 被捕了，而 Electronic Frontier Foundation 大约在那时成立，来帮助保护处在这种处境中的人。Lloyd 被捕后，写了名为 Hackers Manifesto 的东西，我觉得它给出了这个世界正在发生之事的原始版本。

cues.en: So he says, I'm smarter than most other kids. This crap they teach us bores me. I've listened to my teacher explain for the 15th time how to reduce a fraction. I understand it. No, Ms. Smith, I didn't show my work. I did it in my head. And you can see, well, he says, I made a discovery today. I found a computer. It does what I want it to do. If I make a mistake, it's because I screwed up, not because it doesn't like me or it feels threatened by me.
cues.zh: 他说，我比大多数孩子都聪明。他们教我们的那些破玩意儿让我无聊。老师第十五次讲怎么约分，我听了。我懂。不，Smith 老师，我没写过程。我在脑子里算的。你看，他说，今天我有了一个发现。我发现了一台电脑。它按我的意愿做事。如果我犯错，那是因为我搞砸了，不是因为它不喜欢我，或者觉得我威胁到它。

cues.en: or it thinks I'm a smartass, or it doesn't like teaching and shouldn't be here. So you're seeing this guy's 21 when he's writing this. He's somebody sort of very disillusioned, not just with government or big business, but like just his classroom, the social environment he's living in. And he goes on to say, this is our world now. We explore, but you call us criminals. You build atomic bombs, wage wars. He's trying to make us believe it's for our own good, yet we're the criminals.
cues.zh: 或者它觉得我自作聪明，或者它不喜欢教书、不该待在这儿。所以你能看出，这个人写这些时才 21 岁。他有点非常幻灭，不只是对政府或大企业，而是对他所在的课堂、他所处的社会环境。他接着说，这是我们的世界了。我们探索，你却叫我们罪犯。你们造原子弹、发动战争。他们试图让我们相信这是为了我们好，可我们却成了罪犯。

cues.en: So again, you see that explicit distrust of hierarchy. And then finally, my crime is that of outsmarting you, something you will never forgive me for. So I don't know how many people who work on open source will recognize aspects of this attitude and interactions they have. But there's sort of such a strong rejection of the social things going on. It's like, well, the teacher who's not teaching you well has a bunch of other students.
cues.zh: 所以再次，你看到那种对等级制度的明确不信任。最后，我的罪就是比你聪明，这是你永远不会原谅我的事。我不知道有多少做开源的人会认出这种态度以及他们互动中的一些方面。但这里有一种对社会现状的强烈拒绝。就像，那个没教好你的老师还有一堆别的学生。

cues.en: It's difficult to balance all their needs. Maybe it's malicious, but maybe there's another reason. But this worldview is kind of like, I outsmarted you. You don't see it how I see it. So when I take a step back on this intellectual pathway, the things I sort of draw out from reading these books and things is one, we're gods.
cues.zh: 要平衡他们所有人的需求很难。也许是恶意的，但也可能有别的原因。但这种世界观有点像：我比你聪明。你看不到我所看到的。所以当我回望这条思想路径时，我从读这些书之类的东西中大致得出的结论是：第一，我们是神。

cues.en: Two, hierarchy has failed us. There's sort of a deep distrust of hierarchical structures. I think, rightly, there's a lot of bad things that come out of hierarchy. And finally, order will emerge from the new technology. So when we reconsider the patterns we see in open source, stuff makes a lot of sense. So it's like, why don't you just, it's like, having you, like, we can just, through reason and rationality, figure out the answer. Like, why don't you just do the obvious thing?
cues.zh: 第二，等级制度辜负了我们。这里有一种对等级结构的深度不信任。我认为，而且这是有道理的，等级制度会产生很多坏东西。最后，秩序将从新技术中涌现。所以当我们重新审视在开源中看到的模式时，很多事情就说得通了。就像，你为什么不干脆……有了你，我们可以只靠理性和逻辑找出答案。就像，你为什么不直接做显而易见的事？

cues.en: Hierarchy has failed us. So, again, on whose authority is coming out of this tradition of hierarchical structures haven't served us well. We need to find a way that isn't structured in that way. Like your authority as the author is not legitimate on those grounds. And all discussion is constructive. It's like, well, this is the new technology. This is what the new technology is producing. So this must be the way forward to this place that we want to go.
cues.zh: 层级制度辜负了我们。所以，再次重申，质疑“凭谁的权威”正是源于层级结构并未让我们受益这一传统。我们需要找到一种非层级化的组织方式。比如，基于这种理念，你作为作者的权威也是站不住脚的。而且所有的讨论都是建设性的。就像是说：好吧，这就是新技术，这就是新技术带来的成果，所以这必然是通向我们目标的道路。

cues.en: So I found this pathway really interesting and it informed, it helped me understand a lot what was going on, but it's just one of a couple different ways of looking at how we got to this level of conflict in open source. So I'm calling this sort of the intellectual history of freedom. People are primarily prioritizing freedom, but there are other ones such as people who are primarily prioritizing engagement.
cues.zh: 我觉得这个切入点非常有意思，它启发了我，帮我厘清了很多现状，但要理解开源为何会产生如今这种程度的冲突，这只是几种视角之一。我把它称作自由的思想史。许多人把自由放在首位，但也有人主要优先考虑参与度。

cues.en: I want to start with a quote. The enormous expansion of communications has entirely transformed the conditions of trade and commerce. Everything is done in haste at fever pitch, the night is used for travel, the day for business, even holiday trips put strain on the nervous system. Do people relate to that? Holiday trips being stressful? I feel that. Or I struggle with that at least. I try to take a break or whatever. Great political, industrial and financial crises.
cues.zh: 我想先引用一段话。“通讯的巨大飞跃彻底改变了商业贸易的条件。一切都在狂热与匆忙中进行，昼行商务，夜用于奔波，甚至连度假都会让人神经紧绷。”大家有共鸣吗？度假也压力很大？我深有感触。至少我对此深感困扰。我也试着去休个假什么的。“重大的政治、工业与金融危机……”

cues.en: carry this segment into far wider areas of the population than ever before. Interest in political life has become universal. Tempers are inflamed by political, religious, and social struggles, party politics, electioneering. Sound familiar to anybody? Finally, people are forced to engage in a constant mental activity and robbed of the time you defer relaxation, sleep, and rest. So if you had to guess when this was written, it's reasonable. It could be this year.
cues.zh: “……波及到了前所未有广泛的人群。对政治生活的关注变得普及。政治、宗教与社会斗争、政党纷争、拉票竞选，无不激化着情绪。”听起来耳熟吗？“最终，人们被迫持续进行高强度的脑力活动，被剥夺了本该用于放松、睡眠和休息的时间。”如果让你猜这是什么时候写的，很合常理，可能就是今年。

cues.en: It could be 2017, or maybe someone was really prophetic and they wrote it in like 1980. It's like, I see where this is all going. So this is actually from something Freud wrote in 1902. The part I left out is due to the worldwide telegraph and telephone networks and the immense growth of trade unionism. So, I mean, I think it makes sense that he would have seen these kinds of things. He seems like a smart dude, or at least someone who's very sensitive to...
cues.zh: 可能是 2017 年，或者某人极具远见，在 1980 年左右写下的。就像在说：我看到了未来的走向。但这其实出自 Freud 在 1902 年写的一篇文章。我略去的那句是“由于全球电报和电话网络，以及工会主义的迅猛发展”。所以，我觉得他能预见这些完全讲得通。他是个很厉害的人，或者至少对某些事物非常敏锐……

cues.en: human behavior. And so this is kind of where this intellectual history starts. So we have Freud, but we're going to look at two other books. One is called Propaganda from 1928, and one is called Nudge, much more recent, from 2008. So with Propaganda, this is written by Edward Bernays. This is actually Freud's nephew. The connections between all these works are crazy, and as you look into any parts of these,
cues.zh: ……对人类行为。而这也就是这段思想史的起点。除了 Freud，我们还要看另外两本书。一本是 1928 年的《Propaganda》，另一本要近得多，是 2008 年的《Nudge》。《Propaganda》由 Edward Bernays 所著。他其实是 Freud 的外甥。所有这些作品之间的联系简直不可思议，当你深入挖掘其中的任何细节，

cues.en: like everybody met, everybody worked with someone's nephew or cousin or mom or it's very strange. So this book is essentially a bunch of stories about how Edward Bernays sort of created the idea of public relations. So one of the stories he tells is about torches of freedom. So this was an ad campaign to break the taboo against women smoking. At the time men would smoke and it was acceptable to some degree and women couldn't, it was very looked down upon.
cues.zh: 就会发现所有人都认识，大家都跟某人的外甥、表亲或母亲共事过，非常奇妙。这本书基本上讲的都是 Edward Bernays 如何开创“公共关系”概念的故事。其中他讲到了一个关于“自由火炬”（torches of freedom）的故事。这是一场旨在打破女性吸烟禁忌的广告营销活动。当时男性吸烟在某种程度上是可以接受的，而女性则不行，吸烟会被严重鄙视。

cues.en: So the president of the American Tobacco Company said, if we can break this taboo, it'll be like a gold mine opening right in our front yard. So he hires Edward Bernays. And what Edward Bernays does is he hires women who are good looking but not too model-y. That's the quote I found, good looking but not too model-y. To walk in an Easter Sunday parade and smoke.
cues.zh: 美国烟草公司总裁说，如果我们能打破这个禁忌，那就像自家前院开了座金矿。于是他雇了 Edward Bernays。Edward Bernays 的做法是，雇一些长相好看但别太像模特的女性。这是我找到的原话，“长相好看但别太像模特”。让她们在复活节周日游行中边走边抽烟。

cues.en: he also hired photographers to get really good photos of these women, and then distributed those photos through newspaper connections that he had to make sure he got published all around the world. So this Tortures of Freedom idea was saying we see this trend about women's liberation happening, and this is aligned with that movement, and this is a way of punching up against those taboos.
cues.zh: 他还雇了摄影师，给这些女性拍出非常好看的照片，然后通过他在报社的人脉分发这些照片，确保它们能在全世界刊登。所以这个 “Tortures of Freedom” 的点子是说，我们看到女性解放运动正在兴起，这件事与之契合，也是一种冲击那些禁忌的方式。

cues.en: But it's very focused on like, hey, we're going to make a bunch of money here. And so one of the ads that came out of this was, an ancient prejudice has been removed. And what's interesting about this ad is that visually, it's clearly about women smoking. But texturally, it's saying toasting did it. It's because they toast the tobacco, it's less harsh on your throat, and that's what has removed the prejudice. So texturally,
cues.zh: 但它非常聚焦于，嘿，我们要在这儿大赚一笔。于是由此推出的一则广告说，“一种古老的偏见已被消除”。这则广告有趣的地方在于，视觉上明显是在讲女性吸烟，但从文字上看，它说的是烘烤工艺的功劳。因为他们烘烤烟叶，对喉咙刺激更小，正是这一点消除了偏见。所以从文字上，

cues.en: They can say, look, we're not getting into politics. We're just saying that toasting is cool, and that's a lady who smokes. It's like, I don't see the problem. But meanwhile, you have hired Edward Bernays to actually run this campaign. So, oh yeah, I want to read a little bit from his book. This is the book. He says, the old-fashioned propagandist, using almost exclusively the appeal to the printed word, tried to persuade the individual.
cues.zh: 他们可以说，看，我们不是在搞政治。我们只是说烘烤工艺很酷，那是一位抽烟的女士。就像，我看不出有什么问题。但与此同时，你雇了 Edward Bernays 来实际操盘这场宣传。对了，我想从他的书里读一点。就是这本书。他说，老式宣传者几乎只靠诉诸印刷文字，试图说服个人，

cues.en: to buy a definite article immediately. So he's like, his example of this is like, you buy O'Leary's rubber bands now. And he's like, okay, that's the old fashioned way. The modern propagandist therefore sets to work to create the circumstances that will modify the custom. It doesn't matter what this ad says. It's about creating circumstances such that the custom will change in whatever direction someone pays me to change it.
cues.zh: 立刻购买某件特定商品。他的例子就像，“你现在就买 O'Leary's 橡皮筋”。他说，好吧，那是老派做法。因此现代宣传者着手创造能改变习俗的环境。这则广告具体说什么不重要。关键是创造环境，让习俗朝着付钱让我改变的方向变化。

cues.en: So another example he gives is for Mozart pianos. So I don't know exactly the finances of Mozart pianos, but let's say they had 30% of market share, and he gets hired to make it higher. Maybe it can go to 35 or 40. That'd be a huge for Mozart pianos. So Bernays comes in and he says, okay, I could say to people, will you please buy a piano? But I'm not gonna do that. I know that pianos have this sort of elite cache.
cues.zh: 他给出的另一个例子是 Mozart 钢琴。我不清楚 Mozart 钢琴的具体财务状况，但假设他们占 30% 市场份额，他被雇来把份额做高。也许能升到 35% 或 40%。这对 Mozart 钢琴来说会是巨大增长。于是 Bernays 进来说，好，我可以对人们说，请买一架钢琴吧？但我不会那么做。我知道钢琴有那种精英光环。

cues.en: And so what I'm going to do is I'm going to make a architecture expo in New York City where we're going to showcase music parlors and we're going to bring in famous people, influential artists and musicians to be in the rooms. We're going to have expensive tapestries and really lean into this elite picture and promote it in our connections with newspapers. He also invites architects from all over the country. He wants influential architects.
cues.zh: 所以我要做的是，在纽约办一场建筑博览会，在那里展示音乐室，并请名人、有影响力的艺术家和音乐家到场。我们会用昂贵的挂毯，充分营造这种精英图景，并通过报社人脉宣传。他还邀请全国各地的建筑师。他要的是有影响力的建筑师。

cues.en: and they'll bring designs for music parlors. So what this expo does is it creates a music parlor as an aspirational goal, and it brings in architects who will then go back to wherever they're from with designs for music parlors, and they'll start building houses that have that. And ideally, they'll influence other architects who are not as influential to add music parlors as well. And so instead of saying, hey, will you please buy this piano, people are now saying, hey, I have this piano-shaped hole that I need to fill.
cues.zh: 他们会带回琴房的设计方案。所以这个博览会所做的，就是把琴房塑造成一个令人向往的目标，吸引建筑师过来，让他们回到各自的家乡时带上琴房的设计，并在建房子时把琴房加进去。理想情况下，他们还会影响那些名气没那么大的建筑师也加上琴房。这样一来，与其求着别人说“嘿，买台钢琴吧”，大家现在反而会说：“哎呀，我这刚好空出个放钢琴的位置，得填上才行。”

cues.en: something piano-shaped. So again, the modern propagandist sets to work to create the circumstances that will modify the custom. So this got modernized and sort of made a bit nicer in nudge. So this book has been really influential in
cues.zh: 放个刚好能摆钢琴的东西。所以说，现代宣传人员致力于创造足以改变习俗的环境。这个概念后来被现代化，并在《助推》里包装得更温和了些。在这里我们看到，助推是指选择架构中的任何要素，它能在不禁止任何选择、也不显著改变经济激励的情况下，以可预测的方式改变人们的行为。这本书最近在

cues.en: Tech recently. So one thing that we're probably all familiar. That's an example of this is auto play of videos. So you just finished a show. It ends on a cliffhanger because they wrote it that way. And you're like, man, that was that was cool. And you're like, oh, my body. Is it is it hungry? Does it need a walk? Did it have plans for today or for anything?
cues.zh: 科技圈影响非常深远。大家可能都很熟悉一个例子，那就是视频自动播放。你刚看完一集，剧集在悬念处戛然而止，因为编剧就是这么设计的。你心想：“天哪，太精彩了。”然后你又琢磨：“呃，我身体吃得消吗？饿不饿？需要去散个步吗？今天还有别的安排吗？”

cues.en: And then the music starts again, and you're like, no, no. So this is a nudge, right? You're free to do some other behavior. So if anyone's visited Google Cappaterias, you'll probably have seen all the food is marked with colors. So green means eat any time. Yellow means once in a while.
cues.zh: 紧接着片头音乐又响起了，你只能妥协：“算了算了。”这就是助推，对吧？你完全可以自由地去做别的事，但通过精心构建的选择架构，会有可预见比例的人放弃这种自由选择。这种做法在 Google 也流行了起来。如果有人去过 Google 的员工餐厅，大概会发现所有食物都标上了颜色：绿色代表随时可吃，黄色代表偶尔吃吃，

cues.en: red means not often, please. And it's all marked. It's actually very helpful. You can be like, oh, I just had one red thing today. It's kind of nice. But this interest in colors changing people's behavior was used at Google in other ways. So when you look at the history of their ad labeling, you see something similar. So when ads started, they sort of just start by playing around with colors. It's like, whoa, maybe green is fun.
cues.zh: 红色代表“请尽量少吃”。全都标注好了。这其实挺有用的，你会想：“噢，我今天只吃了一样红标食物，挺好的。”但这种利用颜色改变用户行为的心思，在 Google 也被用在了其他地方。只要看看他们广告标识的历史演变，就会发现类似的操作。最初有广告的时候，他们基本上只是在折腾颜色，比如“哇，绿色可能挺好玩的”，

cues.en: Maybe this lavender purple thing is the way to go. So in a new phase of things, you start to see, okay, let's do something more, can it be something more white? Okay, yeah, maybe a little more white, you know? Well, how about something a little more white? All this color is like, let's just put it in one place. We'll take all the saturation, put it in one place. And hey, it works fine, no problem. And then it's like, well,
cues.zh: “或者这种薰衣草紫才是正确的方向”。到了新阶段，你会看到：“好，再改改，能不能更偏白一点？行，也许再白一点，对吧？那再偏白一点怎么样？这些颜色太杂了，干脆集中放一个地方吧，把所有色彩饱和度都堆在一块。”嘿，效果挺好，没毛病。再然后呢，

cues.en: Yellow's pretty ugly. Like, we could just, you know, it's still labeled. It's no problem. And then it's like, I mean, who wanted it to be yellow? And I mean, it wasn't really that important. And then it's like, you know, the background. I mean, people get it. They get it. So when you search for Italy tour, for example, everything above the fold is an ad and it's labeled in this very
cues.zh: “黄色其实挺难看的。其实我们只要保留标识就行了，没问题的。”接着又变成：“话说回来，谁非要用黄色啊？其实根本没那么重要。”然后就是：“那个底色嘛，大家都懂的，用户心里有数。”所以比如当你搜索“意大利旅游”时，首屏展示的全是广告，而且标识得非常

cues.en: subtle and nice way. So I found this very interesting quote from the head of Text Ads at Google. He says, we want to make it easier for our users to adjust information on the page. So we're gradually trying to reduce the number of variations of colors and patterns on the page and bring a little bit more harmony to the page. Like, we just want harmony.
cues.zh: 微妙而自然。我在 Google 文字广告负责人的发言里看到了一段非常耐人寻味的话，他说：“我们希望用户能更轻松地获取页面上的信息。因此，我们正在逐步减少页面上的颜色和图案变化，让页面显得更加和谐。”你看，“我们只是想要页面和谐”。

cues.en: And that's why we reduced one of the color elements on the page. We could have reduced other color elements. It's just one color element. What's the big deal? So some of you may be thinking, Evan, if you're so mad about this, why don't you just change your default search? You typed it into Safari, so clearly that's the default. Well, another thing I learned when I was looking into this is Google paid $1 billion to Apple to keep the search bar on iPhones.
cues.zh: 这就是为什么我们减少了页面上的一个色彩元素。我们本来也可以减少其他色彩元素。不过就一个色彩元素嘛，有什么大不了的？可能有人会想：Evan，你要是这么生气，为什么不直接改掉默认搜索引擎呢？你是在 Safari 里搜的，显然那就是默认设置。好吧，我在查这事时还发现：Google 曾向 Apple 支付了10亿美元，就为了保住 iPhone 上的搜索栏。

cues.en: Furthermore, these sums called traffic acquisition costs rose to $5.5 billion or 23% of ad revenue. So we're in a situation where a choice architecture has been created. You know, the circumstances have been modified such that, you know, well, I don't mind searching in this way, or I could scroll down below these ads, but I don't really want to.
cues.zh: 不仅如此，这些被称为流量获取成本的支出后来涨到了55亿美元，占到了广告收入的23%。所以我们面临的局面是，一种“选择架构”被建立起来了。环境被刻意改造成这样——你知道的，就是“其实我也不介意这么搜”，或者“我本可以往下翻跳过这些广告，但我真不太想翻”。

cues.en: So the circumstances have been created such that custom is modified. And if we wanted to mess with this, it's going to cost a lot of money, right? The fact that DuckDuckDuck exists doesn't mean that they can compete with these kinds of numbers. So I think this whole intellectual lineage leads to something that we see in online communities a lot, which is things are viral by design.
cues.zh: 所以环境就是这么被塑造出来的，以至于习惯都被改变了。如果我们想撼动这一点，代价会非常高昂，对吧？DuckDuckDuck 的存在，并不意味着他们有能力和这种体量的数据抗衡。所以我认为，这一整套思想脉络导向了我们在网络社区中屡见不鲜的现象——事物在设计之初就是为了病毒式传播。

cues.en: So when Bernays starts an advertising campaign, all these stories he tells, he always starts with a psychological hook. So you might observe that people process emotions by sharing them with others. So that might look like, you know, someone's going about their day. It's fine. And someone shows up and they're like, that work you did last week, it was terrible. Like, it's not going to work out. It was really not carefully considered. And that person feels sad.
cues.zh: 当 Bernays 发起广告营销活动时，在他讲的所有故事里，开头总是带着心理诱饵。你可能会发现，人们消化情绪的方式是与他人分享。比如某人正平平静静地过着一天，突然有人冒出来说：“你上周做的工作烂透了。根本行不通，考虑得太不周全了。”这个人就会感到难过。

cues.en: And that person goes, the person yelling at them goes away. So they might mope around for a day or however long. And hopefully they run into a friend who hears the story and they're like, oh man, that sucks. But you know, I don't think that was really fair assessment like, and through talking it through, the person can sort of deal with that and move through. Another interaction that might be possible is you're going about your day and someone says, did you hear about that terrible thing that's happening over there? And you say, whoa, that's terrible.
cues.zh: 接着骂人的那个人走开了。挨骂的人可能会郁闷上一整天甚至更久。幸运的话，他们碰到了一个朋友，朋友听了之后会说：“天呐，太糟了。但我认为这评价不太客观……”通过倾诉交流，这个人就能排解情绪并走出来。而另一种可能发生的互动是：你正过着平常的一天，有人对你说：“你听说了那边发生的那件破事吗？”你会说：“哇，那太糟糕了。”

cues.en: And then you see a friend and you say, hey, did you hear about that? And they're like, oh, that's terrible. And they see some of their friends. And they're like, man, that thing over there is really bad. Viral. So when we're choosing what kind of messages we want to put into society to control it, as the cyberneticist might say, this one has a very interesting pattern. So when you get something that has a viral reaction, that's something that has more engagement.
cues.zh: 然后你见到了一个朋友并说：“嘿，你听说了那事吗？”对方也会觉得：“天呐，太可怕了。”接着他们又见到了自己的朋友，说：“伙计，那边发生的事真的太恶劣了。”这就是病毒式传播。所以，正如控制论学者可能会说的，当我们选择向社会注入何种信息以实施控制时，这种模式非常有意思。只要你制造出能引发病毒式反应的内容，就能获得更高的用户参与度。

cues.en: a lot of people who are running Silicon Valley companies in an idealistic way. They want to make the world better through tools. They're put in this choice architecture where it's like you have these investors and you don't want to disappoint them. There's all these people who work at your company. You don't want to lay them off. So do you want hashtag disappointing Q3? Or do you want the viral one? So once you have this psychological hook, you can start designing ways to make it work better.
cues.zh: 很多以理想主义方式经营硅谷公司的人，想通过工具让世界变好。他们被置于这种选择架构中：你有这些投资人，你不想让他们失望。公司里还有这么多员工，你不想裁掉他们。所以你是想要#令人失望的Q3，还是想要那个病毒式传播的？一旦有了这种心理钩子，你就可以开始设计让它更好地运作的方法。

cues.en: So the ones I sort of noticed have been to mix extremes. So if we come back to our priorities graph of different people, these people don't necessarily congregate in the same place. But what we really want to happen is for the most extreme people to yell at each other as aggressively as possible. And so one way to do that might be to put all the different programming communities in one place. So if you look at sort of different online discussion forums,
cues.zh: 所以我注意到的一类做法，是把极端者混在一起。回到不同人的优先级图，这些人未必聚集在同一处。但我们真正想要的是，让最极端的人尽可能激烈地互相吼。做到这一点的一种方式，可能是把所有不同的编程社区放到同一个地方。所以如果你看看各种不同的在线讨论论坛，

cues.en: I think the degree to which different communities collide will predict the amount of conflict that you see there. So on Hacker News, I find that the sort of most difficult and most combative place. And then on the R programming, you'll see more of that. And on the subreddits for individual languages, you'll see less. On places that are just community places that don't have accounts that are shared between, you'll see less. So another approach is to decontextualize the person.
cues.zh: 我认为不同社区碰撞的程度，会预测你在那里看到的冲突量。在 Hacker News 上，我发现那是最难搞、最好斗的地方。然后在 R 编程社区，你会看到更多这种情况。在各个语言的 subreddit 上，你会看到更少。在那些只是社区场所、账号不互通的地方，你会看到更少。所以另一种方法是把人剥离语境。

cues.en: So instead of two people talking, you have Tango Dango talking to Foxtrot. And what's interesting here is when they saw each other's faces, they might be able to say, oh, this person isn't trying to be malicious. They feel this way. But when it's Tango Dango, it could literally be Hitler. It could. You don't know. He's just in Argentina being like, infix operators are stupid. Unclean.
cues.zh: 所以不是两个人在说话，而是 Tango Dango 在跟 Foxtrot 说话。有趣的是，当他们看到彼此的脸时，可能会说：哦，这个人并不是想恶意。他就是这样感受的。但如果是 Tango Dango，那完全可能是希特勒。真有可能。你不知道。他就在阿根廷说：中缀运算符很蠢。不干净。

cues.en: So another way to decontextualize things is to limit the amount of characters that are available to people. Another way is to limit the kind of feedback that's available. So instead of saying, hey, that was pretty hurtful, you say, down. Like a lot of nuance is lost in that sort of thing. So when I take a step back on all this, I think there's a big conflict here where there's very powerful incentives for our interactions to go really poorly. And I don't think the
cues.zh: 所以另一种剥离语境的方式，是限制人们可用的字符数。另一种方式是限制可用的反馈类型。于是不是说“嘿，这挺伤人的”，而是说“踩”。这种机制里会丢失很多细微差别。所以当我退一步看这一切，我认为这里有一个大冲突：有非常强大的激励让我们的互动变得很糟。而且我不认为

cues.en: intellectual history of freedom really is well set up to protect against that. Like if you are living in a choice architecture that predictably alters people's behavior, yeah, you were given a free choice, but you happen to choose a different thing 30% of the time. So this got me interested in a different pathway. So I ask a lot, why don't I have any of these problems in person? So like at work or at conferences or at meetups or on the street.
cues.zh: 自由的思想史真的能很好地防范这一点。比如，如果你生活在一个能可预测地改变人行为的选择架构中，是的，你得到了自由选择，但你恰好在 30% 的时候选了不同的东西。这让我对另一条路径产生兴趣。所以我经常问，为什么我面对面时没有这些问题？比如在工作时、在会议上、在聚会上，或在街上。

cues.en: All these places are for something. So when a place is for something, you can ask what's inappropriate behavior. If I'm at work and a discussion keeps going and going, at some point it's like we have to stop having the discussion and make a choice. We can't be in discussion forever. It's clear because the work is for work. And at a conference, you know, it's against the norms to jump up on a stage and being like, that's wrong.
cues.zh: 所有这些场所都是为了某种目的。所以当一个场所是为了某种目的时，你就可以问什么是不合适的行为。如果我在工作，而讨论一直拖下去，到了某个时候就像是，我们必须停止讨论并做出选择。我们不能永远讨论下去。这很清楚，因为工作就是为了工作。而在会议上，你知道，跳上台说“那是错的”是违反规范的。

cues.en: The idea is you carefully select speakers who might have something interesting to say to folks and try to efficiently and in a nice way present that. At a meetup, if someone's being really aggressive, they're always just saying, oh, I need to go to the bathroom. There's ways out of those kinds of conflicts and you're talking face to face. On the street, someone's standing outside Starbucks and being like, I had better coffee one time. It's like, that's weird. That's weird behavior.
cues.zh: 这个想法是，你要仔细挑选可能对大家有有趣内容可讲的演讲者，并尝试高效且友好地呈现出来。在聚会上，如果有人非常咄咄逼人，他们总是只说，哦，我得去趟洗手间。这类冲突有办法脱身，而且你们是面对面交谈。在街上，有人站在星巴克外面说，我有一次喝过更好的咖啡。这就像是，那很奇怪。那是很奇怪的行为。

cues.en: And the croissants could be done better. I don't know how, but they could. This isn't it. So this idea of a place being for something I think is really important. And so I had this idea for intentional communication. And so the idea is that instead of just having a blank box you write into, you first choose some intent. My intent is to learn, let's say. And I'll get prompted to say, OK, what's your background? Maybe they started using Elm.
cues.zh: 而且可颂可以做得更好。我不知道怎么做得更好，但确实可以。不是这个。所以我认为“场所是为了某种目的”这个想法真的很重要。于是我就有了“有意图的沟通”这个想法。这个想法是，你不再只是有一个空白框往里写，而是先选择某种意图。比如说，我的意图是学习。然后我会被提示说，好，你的背景是什么？也许他们开始用 Elm。

cues.en: And they've been doing Java for a long time. And the question is, why do I have to explicitly cast between ints and float when doing math? And then I can submit the post. So when that shows up, this question might have been read in a combative way. Like, why do I have to explicitly cast between ints and float when doing math? Or like, why do I have to explicitly cast between? Like, both of those are valid interpretations of this text. But when you give some background,
cues.zh: 而且他们做 Java 很久了。问题是，为什么我在做数学运算时必须在 int 和 float 之间显式转换？然后我就可以提交帖子。所以当它出现时，这个问题可能会被读成一种对抗性的语气。比如，为什么我在做数学运算时必须在 int 和 float 之间显式转换？或者像，为什么我必须显式转换？这两个都是这段文本的合理解读。但当你给出一些背景时，

cues.en: It's like, okay, I see where this person is coming from. I can see why they'd be frustrated with that, and it's really harder to read it in a malicious way. So instead of just having a reply button, maybe you can say, okay, I can either ask for clarification or I can give an answer. And so if I say I'm gonna give an answer, again, we might have this structured way of replying. Restate the question, answer it, and then...
cues.zh: 就像是，好吧，我明白这个人是从什么角度出发的。我能理解他们为什么会对此感到沮丧，而且真的更难把它解读成恶意。所以与其只有一个回复按钮，也许你可以说，好吧，我可以要求澄清，或者我可以给出答案。那么如果我说我要给出答案，同样，我们可能会有这种结构化的回复方式。重述问题，回答它，然后……

cues.en: We can say hey we value citations we value like people backing up with evidence or experience so maybe they give a citation and they can post it. And so again you get the answer and the person asking says oh that's not the question I was asking actually so that can really help clarify and make this process more efficient. So again instead of reply maybe you say ask for clarification or thank the person. And so there's a couple of things you can add to this I think that would help.
cues.zh: 我们可以说，嘿，我们重视引用，我们重视人们用证据或经验来支撑，所以也许他们给出一个引用，然后就可以发布。这样你又得到了答案，而提问的人说，哦，那其实不是我问的问题，所以这真的能帮助澄清，让这个过程更高效。所以同样，与其回复，也许你说要求澄清，或者感谢对方。所以我觉得你可以在这个基础上加几样东西，会有帮助。

cues.en: So one is the idea of conversation flows. So we saw someone wants to learn. You can clarify your answer if you choose to answer. They can ask clarifying question or thank you. Now if they clarify maybe you give another answer. But in the other pathways say hey maybe can you give me an example to clarify your question. They can restate it and then you can answer. So the point here is just that yell angrily isn't one of the states in the discussion. It's unreachable.
cues.zh: 其中之一是对话流程这个思路。比如我们看到有人想学习。如果你选择回答，可以先澄清你的回答。他们可以提出澄清性问题，或者道谢。现在如果他们澄清了，也许你会再给一个回答。但在其他路径里，比如“嘿，能不能举个例子来澄清你的问题”。他们可以重述问题，然后你再回答。所以这里的重点只是，愤怒地大喊并不是讨论中的状态之一。它是不可达的。

cues.en: So this isn't to say that all discussion should be this way, because there are places where you want self-expression. You say, hey, I had a really nice time at the park. Here's a photo of it. And someone says, oh, that's great. That reminds me of last week we were clicking something really nice. And so you can have these cycles. But when someone's doing self-expression, you're saying, man, that's really like a terrible thing to say. Maybe you could have a conversation flow that says, hey, I want to learn about that perspective. I don't want to tell you it's wrong. I just want to know why you feel that way.
cues.zh: 这并不是说所有讨论都得是这种模式，因为有些场合大家只是想表达自我。比如你说：“嘿，我今天在公园玩得超开心，给你们看张照片。”然后有人说：“哇，太棒了，这让我想起上周我们拍到的精彩瞬间。”这种互动很正常。但如果有人在自我表达时，你却说：“天哪，这话也太难听了吧。”或许我们可以换一种对话节奏：“嘿，我想了解一下你的视角，我不是想说你不对，只是想知道你为什么会有这种感受。”

cues.en: So what might be interesting here is, like, the discussion flows will be different depending on the goals of the community, right? If it's about learning, it might be one way. If it's about self-expression, it might be another way. And maybe you want safety valves to jump around. So another thing that I think is interesting is, say a discussion's happening and it's getting really out of control, and it's like, hey, this is nice. And then by the end, they're like, your mom is a bad person, and she, you know, threw a bicycle on the ground.
cues.zh: 所以这里很有意思的一点是，讨论的走向会因社区的目标而不同，对吧？如果是为了学习，可能是一种形式；如果是为了自我表达，可能是另一种形式；也许你还会需要一些安全阀机制来灵活跳转。另外我觉得挺有意思的是，假设一场讨论正在进行，然后彻底失控了，本来开头大家还觉得“嘿，这挺不错的”，结果到最后却变成了“你妈不是个好人，而且她还把自行车摔地上了”这种攻击。

cues.en: I don't know. So this is where you don't really want things to go. So one thing that might be interesting is when you see someone about to reply, say, hey, what would be a successful conclusion to this interaction? Or would it be easier to chat for five minutes? Is there somewhere to take this that's going to be more constructive? What do you want to get out of this? Another thing that might be really valuable. So we talked about upvote, downvote stuff.
cues.zh: 我不知道。情况变成这样并不是大家想看到的。所以有个挺有意思的思路：当你看到有人正准备回复时，不妨问一句：“嘿，这次交流怎样才算圆满？”或者直接聊个五分钟会不会更省事？能不能把讨论引向更有建设性的方向？你究竟想从中得到什么？还有一点可能非常有价值，我们之前聊到了点赞、点踩那些机制。

cues.en: When someone gets downvoted, they think to themselves, these people just can't take it. I outsmarted them, and they can't accept that. But the people might actually be saying, man, that was pretty rude and uncalled for. And so that feedback's not reaching that person, and they feel increasingly alienated by these kinds of reactions. Furthermore, these buttons sort of uniquely pick out, like, ah, I'm mad. Oh, I like that. So what we might be able to do instead is say, hey, for any post,
cues.zh: 当有人被点踩时，他们会想：这些人就是接受不了。我比他们聪明，他们没法接受。但那些人实际可能在说：天哪，这也太粗鲁、太过分了。所以这个反馈传不到那个人那里，他们会因为这类反应越来越觉得被疏远。而且这些按钮会特别挑出某种情绪，比如“啊，我生气了”“哦，我喜欢这个”。所以我们也许可以换个做法，说：嘿，对任何帖子，

cues.en: Here's a couple things that you might notice about it. Is it off topic? Is it helpful? And if the goal of the place is to help professionals, maybe these are the ones you want to choose. But if the goal is helping beginners, maybe you want to choose scary versus encouraging or confusing versus clear. And if the place is about self expression, maybe you want to choose funny and downer. So there's a bunch of extras I'm running out of time, so I'm going to skip. But there's a lot of cool things to do here.
cues.zh: 关于这点，大家可能会注意到几个维度：它跑题了吗？有帮助吗？如果这个平台的目标是帮助专业人士，也许你会想选这些维度。但如果目标是帮助初学者，你可能更想选择“让人望而生畏”还是“令人鼓舞”，或是“令人困惑”还是“清晰明了”。而如果这里主打自我表达，你可能想选“幽默风趣”还是“扫兴消沉”。这里还有很多额外的内容，因为时间快到了，我就先跳过了。不过，这里其实还有很多很酷的事情可以做。

cues.en: So, some people may be looking at this and thinking, if a planned culture necessarily meant uniform, like, hey, like, all this planning is gonna ruin these communities. So, I found this book, it says, if planned culture necessarily meant uniforming and regimentation, it might indeed work against further evolution. If men were very much alike, they would be less likely to hit upon or design new practices, and a culture which made people as much alike as possible might slip into a standard pattern from which there would be no escape.
cues.zh: 所以，有些人看到这个可能会想：如果一种计划性文化必然意味着统一，比如，嘿，这么多规划会毁掉这些社区。于是我找到这本书，它说：如果计划性文化必然意味着统一化和整齐划一，那它可能确实会阻碍进一步演化。如果人们彼此非常相似，他们就不太可能碰巧发现或设计出新的做法，而一种尽可能让人变得相似的文化，可能会滑入一种标准模式，再也无法逃脱。

cues.en: That would be bad design, but if we are looking for a variety, we should not fall back on accident. Many accidental cultures have been marked by uniformity and regimentation. So this is from a book called Beyond Freedom and Dignity by B.F. Skinner, and I think this is one of the clearest books that's sort of recognizing that there are these people who understand choice architectures and that freedom doesn't help you escape from choice architectures, like design of other choice architectures is a way to deal with that.
cues.zh: 那会是个糟糕的设计，但如果我们想要多样性，就不该退而依赖偶然。许多偶然形成的文化都带有统一化和整齐划一的特征。这来自 B.F. Skinner 的《Beyond Freedom and Dignity》一书，我认为它是最清楚地指出这一点的一本书之一：有些人懂得选择架构，而自由并不能帮你逃出选择架构；设计其他选择架构才是应对办法。

cues.en: Ultimately, I'm not here to say, like, here's one way that's right or the others. It's like people are going to have different priorities depending on, you know, their life and their experiences. I think the point that's important is that there's a lot of people in open source communities who are getting hurt, right? So, like, it's hard emotionally to work on these kinds of projects. You see people around you getting hurt. And just saying, well, people are just expressing themselves isn't solving the question, and we have these very...
cues.zh: 归根结底，我不是来说某一种方式就是对的、其他方式就是错的。人们会根据自己的人生和经历有不同的优先级。我认为重要的一点是，开源社区里有很多人正在受到伤害，对吧？所以，做这类项目在情感上很难。你看到身边的人受到伤害。只说“人们只是在表达自己”并不能解决问题，而且我们有这些非常……

cues.en: people controlling billions of dollars who have particular goals for what happens in these communities.
